title: Module 9 Mastery Gate — Imaging, Virtual Care, and PGHD
instructions: Sprint-11 expanded gate covering enterprise imaging (q1–q10), telemedicine (q11–q15), and RPM/PGHD (q16–q20). Lessons 4–5 (FHIR Bulk Data, SaMD/HTI-1) and their items are added in Sprint 12. Read every rationale.

questions.prompt: A new MRI scanner is brought online and the technologists complain that they have to retype the patient name, MRN, accession number, and exam description at the modality console for every study. Three weeks later the radiology PACS administrator reports a spike in studies that cannot be auto-routed to the right radiologist worklist because of typos and mismatched patient identifiers. Which DICOM service was almost certainly never wired up?
options: C-STORE
C-FIND
DICOM Modality Worklist (MWL)
Storage Commitment
questions.rationale: DICOM Modality Worklist is the query the modality makes to the RIS or EHR to retrieve the day's scheduled exams with patient demographics already populated. When MWL is missing, technologists retype, and retyping is the single largest source of patient-identification errors and downstream routing failures in imaging. C-STORE pushes the acquired image to the PACS — useful but unrelated to the demographic-typing problem. C-FIND is a query for studies already stored. Storage Commitment is the handshake by which the modality confirms the PACS has accepted long-term custody of the image. The 'technologists are retyping' stem is the canonical MWL question.

questions.prompt: A health system that has grown by acquisition now operates four PACS from three vendors across radiology, cardiology, and a recently acquired outpatient imaging center. Clinicians want a single longitudinal view of every image for every patient regardless of where it was acquired, and the CIO wants to be able to replace any one PACS without an image-migration project. Which architectural component most directly addresses both needs?
options: A larger PACS from the dominant vendor
A vendor-neutral archive (VNA) sitting behind the existing PACS systems
An additional integration engine instance
Migrating all images to the EHR's blob storage
questions.rationale: A VNA stores DICOM (and increasingly non-DICOM) imaging objects in a standards-based way independent of any one PACS, with a unified patient/study index across departments. Clinicians get the longitudinal view through a universal viewer that pulls from the VNA; the CIO gains the ability to swap a PACS without re-acquiring or re-migrating the underlying images, because the source of truth is the VNA, not the PACS database. A bigger single-vendor PACS reproduces the lock-in. An integration engine moves messages, not images. Putting images in EHR blob storage abandons DICOM metadata, breaks viewers, and is not a real architecture.

questions.prompt: Two competing health systems in the same metropolitan area want to share imaging studies so that an emergency department at one system can retrieve a recent CT performed at the other without phoning the film library. They want a vendor-neutral, profile-defined approach with a registry/repository pattern they can also extend to documents later. Which IHE profile family fits the requirement?
options: PIX/PDQ
ATNA
XDS-I.b (with XDS for documents)
XUA
questions.rationale: Cross-Enterprise Document Sharing for Imaging (XDS-I.b) is the IHE profile for exactly this use case — publishing imaging studies into a registry/repository so that other organizations can discover and retrieve them across enterprise boundaries. It pairs naturally with the document-side XDS profile when the same infrastructure is reused for clinical documents. PIX/PDQ solves identity reconciliation, ATNA solves audit and node authentication, and XUA carries user identity assertions — all are necessary supporting profiles in a real deployment, but none is the answer to 'how do we share imaging studies cross-enterprise.' The boards want you to know XDS-I by name.

questions.prompt: In the same cross-enterprise imaging deployment, the two health systems realize they assign their own MRNs to patients and that the same person may be MRN 12345 at one system and MRN 98765 at the other. Which IHE profile is designed to reconcile these identifiers across the participating systems?
options: PIX (Patient Identifier Cross-Reference)
ATNA (Audit Trail and Node Authentication)
XUA (Cross-Enterprise User Assertion)
XDS-I.b
questions.rationale: PIX is the IHE profile that maintains a cross-reference between MRN spaces across institutions, returning the set of identifiers that all refer to the same person. PDQ is the related demographic-search profile. ATNA addresses audit and node TLS authentication — necessary for HIPAA compliance but unrelated to identity reconciliation. XUA carries the *user's* identity (e.g., the requesting clinician), not the patient's. XDS-I.b governs the imaging exchange itself but assumes identity has already been resolved. Reading the stem carefully — 'reconcile identifiers' — uniquely points to PIX.

questions.prompt: A HIPAA Security Rule audit at a hospital with a deployed IHE infrastructure flags a single weakness: although TLS is enabled between nodes, audit events for PHI access are scattered across each application's local log files in inconsistent formats. Which IHE profile would, if fully implemented, most directly address this finding?
options: PIX
ATNA
XDS-I.b
PDQ
questions.rationale: ATNA (Audit Trail and Node Authentication) does two things: it requires TLS between nodes (already in place here) and it requires every node to emit standardized audit events to a central audit record repository in a defined format (RFC 3881 / DICOM Supplement 95 syslog audit messages). The finding in the stem is precisely the second half of ATNA. PIX, PDQ, and XDS-I.b are unrelated to audit logging. The boards reward you for knowing that ATNA is two things, not one, and that the audit half is often the part organizations forget.

questions.prompt: A radiologist's home reading workstation needs to retrieve a CT study from the hospital PACS. The workstation issues a query to find the study, then asks the PACS to send the study directly back to the workstation itself. Which two DIMSE services has the workstation used, in order?
options: C-STORE then C-FIND
C-FIND then C-MOVE
C-FIND then C-GET
C-MOVE then C-STORE
questions.rationale: C-FIND queries the PACS for matching studies and returns metadata. C-GET asks the PACS to return the actual image objects to the *requesting* node over the same association — appropriate when the requester wants the images itself. C-MOVE is similar but instructs the PACS to send the images to a *third* node (named in the request), which is the more common pattern in classical PACS-to-workstation workflows. The stem specifies 'directly back to the workstation itself,' which is the C-GET pattern. C-STORE is the push direction — modality to PACS — and is not used to *retrieve*. The boards expect you to be able to walk through the four DIMSE services and pick the right one for a described workflow.

questions.prompt: A vendor proposes a browser-based zero-footprint imaging viewer that runs on tablets used at the bedside. The viewer must retrieve DICOM studies from the existing PACS but cannot speak the legacy DIMSE TCP protocol. Which standard set should the viewer use to communicate with the PACS?
options: DICOMweb (WADO-RS, QIDO-RS, STOW-RS)
HL7 v2 ORU messages
FHIR ImagingStudy resources only
Vendor-proprietary REST API
questions.rationale: DICOMweb is the web-services version of DICOM, designed exactly for this case: HTTP-based retrieval (WADO-RS), query (QIDO-RS), and storage (STOW-RS) of DICOM objects, consumable from a browser without DIMSE. HL7 v2 ORU carries result reports, not images. FHIR ImagingStudy is a metadata reference resource that points to images but does not transport pixels — it complements DICOMweb rather than replacing it. A vendor-proprietary REST API would solve the immediate problem but creates lock-in and is the wrong board answer when a standards-based option exists.

questions.prompt: A new CMIO surveys the organization and finds that radiology images live in a PACS, cardiology images in a separate cardiology PACS, dermatology and ophthalmology images in departmental databases the EHR cannot read, point-of-care ultrasound images on the SD cards in the probes themselves, and pathology slides in a research server. The CMIO proposes an 'enterprise imaging' strategy. Which of the following BEST captures what enterprise imaging actually requires?
options: Replacing every departmental system with a single PACS from one vendor
Shared identity, a common imaging archive (typically a VNA), a universal viewer, and governed image-acquisition workflows for non-DICOM modalities such as photography
Migrating all images into the EHR database
Forcing every department to install DICOM modalities
questions.rationale: Enterprise imaging is a discipline, not a product. Its components are shared identity (so the same patient resolves the same way across radiology, cardiology, derm, and pathology), a unified archive (the VNA pattern) so images are not stranded in departmental silos, a universal viewer so clinicians have one interface, and governed acquisition workflows for the long tail of non-DICOM imaging (smartphone wound photography, endoscopy, point-of-care ultrasound). Single-vendor PACS replacement reproduces lock-in at enterprise scale. Putting images in the EHR database abandons DICOM metadata and viewers. Forcing DICOM on every device is unrealistic; the real answer is to bring non-DICOM into governed workflows, not to force the world to be radiology.

questions.prompt: A research team requests a 'de-identified' DICOM study and receives a file with the patient name removed. A privacy officer reviewing the file flags it as still containing identifying information. Which DICOM characteristic most likely explains the privacy officer's concern?
options: DICOM files cannot be de-identified.

The DICOM header contains many additional identifier-bearing tags (accession number, study date, institution, device serial, referring physician, patient ID, study and series UIDs) and may also contain pixel-burned text overlays — removing 'patient name' alone is insufficient.
The pixel data itself is intrinsically identifying.
The DICOM file uses the patient name as a primary key and cannot function without it.
questions.rationale: A DICOM object is a structured container with dozens of metadata tags that can carry identifiers — accession number, study date, institution name and address, device manufacturer and serial number, referring physician name, patient ID, and the UID hierarchy. In addition, ultrasound, fluoroscopy, and many other modalities can burn patient identifiers directly into the pixel data as text overlays. Real DICOM de-identification follows DICOM Supplement 142 (PS 3.15 Annex E), which defines profiles for which tags must be removed, replaced, or hashed, and may also require pixel-region blackout. Removing the patient name is the beginning of the work, not the end. The boards test whether you understand that DICOM 'de-identification' is structurally harder than removing one field.

questions.prompt: In three or four sentences, explain why a vendor-neutral archive (VNA) is the architectural answer to PACS vendor lock-in, and name one risk the VNA pattern does NOT solve.
questions.rationale: A complete answer should observe that historically a PACS stored images in a vendor-proprietary database such that replacing the PACS required a multi-month image-migration project, often with metadata loss, which gave the incumbent vendor enormous renewal leverage. A VNA stores DICOM objects in a standards-based archive (DICOM-conformant storage with preserved metadata) that is independent of any one PACS, so the PACS becomes a viewer/workflow layer over a shared archive and can be replaced without moving the underlying images. The risk a VNA does NOT solve is universal viewer parity (different viewers render and tool studies differently), cross-enterprise sharing (which still requires IHE XDS-I or similar), or identity reconciliation across departments (still a PIX-style problem), or governance of non-DICOM imaging acquisition. Credit any one of these as the named unsolved risk.

questions.prompt: A primary care clinician wants to send a photograph of a suspicious skin lesion, along with a brief history, to a dermatologist who will review and reply within 48 hours. No real-time interaction is required. Which telemedicine modality is described?
options: Synchronous video
Store-and-forward
Remote patient monitoring
E-consult
questions.rationale: Asynchronous transmission of clinical information (in this case, a photograph plus history) for later specialist review is the textbook definition of store-and-forward telemedicine. Teledermatology is the canonical example. Synchronous video would require real-time interaction, which the stem explicitly excludes. RPM is the asynchronous collection of physiologic data from home devices over time, not a one-shot specialist consultation. E-consult is clinician-to-clinician (PCP asks a specialist a question without a patient encounter), and while the stem is close to e-consult in feel, the clinical artifact being transmitted (a lesion photo for diagnosis) makes it store-and-forward teledermatology — the patient is the subject of the consultation, not just the topic.

questions.prompt: A psychiatrist wants to start a new patient on a Schedule II stimulant for ADHD via a synchronous video visit, without any prior in-person evaluation. Which federal statute most directly governs whether this is permissible, and what was its historical default rule?
options: HIPAA Privacy Rule; controlled substance prescribing requires written patient authorization
21st Century Cures Act; controlled substance prescribing is allowed under the information-blocking exceptions

Ryan Haight Online Pharmacy Consumer Protection Act of 2008; historically required at least one in-person evaluation by a DEA-registered prescriber before any controlled substance could be prescribed via telemedicine, with COVID-era flexibilities and a still-evolving permanent DEA framework
MACRA; the Quality Payment Program rules govern controlled substance prescribing
questions.rationale: Ryan Haight is the named federal statute governing controlled substance prescribing via telemedicine. Its historical default required at least one in-person evaluation by a DEA-registered prescriber before any controlled substance could be telemedically prescribed. The COVID PHE waived that requirement; DEA has since proposed and partially finalized a more permanent framework, with buprenorphine for opioid use disorder treated more permissively. HIPAA governs privacy and security, not controlled substances. The Cures Act governs information blocking and APIs. MACRA governs payment, not prescribing authority. The stem is the canonical Ryan Haight question and the boards reuse it nearly verbatim.

questions.prompt: A physician licensed in Pennsylvania wants to provide synchronous video visits to her established patients who have moved to Florida, Arizona, and Colorado. Which of the following is the MOST accurate statement about her licensing requirements?
options: A federal license issued by HHS now permits cross-state telemedicine without additional state licensure.

She must be licensed in each state where her patients are physically located at the time of the encounter; the Interstate Medical Licensure Compact (IMLC) offers an expedited pathway for physicians who hold a full unrestricted license in their state of principal license to obtain additional state licenses, but does not create a single national license.
If the patients were originally established in Pennsylvania, her Pennsylvania license follows them to any state.
The Ryan Haight Act preempts state licensure for telemedicine encounters.
questions.rationale: U.S. physicians are licensed by state, and to practice medicine via telemedicine you must be licensed in the state where the patient is physically located at the time of the encounter, not the state where the clinician sits. The IMLC is the structural workaround — an expedited multi-state pathway for qualifying physicians — but it is not a single federal license, and it requires the physician to actually obtain the additional state licenses, not merely to be eligible. There is no federal medical license in the U.S. The 'license follows the patient' notion is a common misconception with no legal basis. Ryan Haight governs controlled substances, not licensure preemption.

questions.prompt: A state legislature passes a law requiring all commercial insurers to cover telehealth services as a benefit if the same service would be covered when delivered in person, but the law is silent on the rate at which telehealth services must be paid. Which type of telehealth parity has been enacted, and what is the practical implication?
options: Payment parity — telehealth must be paid at the in-person rate.

Coverage parity only — the service must be a covered benefit if delivered via telehealth, but insurers may pay a lower rate, which often determines whether telemedicine programs are financially sustainable.
Both coverage and payment parity, by federal preemption.
Neither — silence on rate means the law is unenforceable.
questions.rationale: Telehealth parity laws come in two distinct forms — coverage parity (the service must be a covered benefit if delivered via telehealth) and payment parity (the rate must equal the in-person rate). A state can mandate one without the other, and the absence of payment parity often determines whether a telemedicine program is financially sustainable: a program may be 'covered' but reimbursed at 60–70% of the in-person rate, which can collapse the business case. The boards reward you for distinguishing the two and for understanding the financial consequence. Federal preemption is not the mechanism here, and a coverage-parity-only law is fully enforceable as a coverage requirement.

questions.prompt: Before the COVID public health emergency, traditional Medicare generally required a beneficiary to be physically located at a specific qualified site (such as a rural health clinic or a physician office in a Health Professional Shortage Area) to receive Medicare-covered telehealth. What is this requirement called?
options: The Ryan Haight in-person requirement
The originating site rule
The IMLC restriction
The HIPAA covered-entity rule
questions.rationale: The originating site rule is the historical Medicare requirement that the beneficiary be physically located at a qualified originating site — typically rural health clinics, hospitals, or physician offices in HPSAs — to receive Medicare-covered telehealth. The rule effectively excluded the patient's home and most urban areas from Medicare telehealth coverage before 2020. The COVID PHE waived the originating site restrictions and allowed the home as an originating site; subsequent legislation has extended those waivers. Ryan Haight is the controlled-substance statute. IMLC is the licensure compact. The HIPAA covered-entity rule is unrelated. The boards expect you to recognize 'originating site' as the named concept.

questions.prompt: A heart failure RPM program is billing CPT 99454 (the monthly device-supply and data-transmission code) and a compliance audit flags a recurring issue: in many months the program billed 99454 for patients who had transmitted readings on only 12 of the 30 days. Which threshold has the program failed to meet, and what is the correct response?
options: There is no minimum-readings threshold for 99454; the audit is incorrect.

99454 requires at least 16 days of readings in the 30-day period; the program must either re-engage patients before day 20 to reach the threshold or not bill 99454 in months when the threshold is not met.
99454 requires 30 consecutive days of readings without exception.
99454 requires only that the device be supplied; transmission days are not counted.
questions.rationale: CPT 99454 requires at least 16 days of physiologic data transmissions in a 30-day period. It is the most common RPM compliance failure in audits, and well-run programs build a vendor-side report that flags any patient at risk of falling below the threshold by day 20 so the team can re-engage the patient before the billing window closes. Billing 99454 in a month where the patient transmitted 12 days exposes the program to recoupment. The boards do not test the four-digit code itself but they do test the 16-day threshold concept.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a true statement about CPT 99457?
options: It pays for the first 20 minutes per calendar month of clinical staff time spent reviewing RPM data and managing the patient, and requires at least one interactive (typically synchronous) communication with the patient during the month.
It pays for the device supply only.
It is a one-time setup code billed at program enrollment.
It may be billed without any patient interaction.
questions.rationale: 99457 is the base management-time code for RPM — the first 20 minutes per calendar month of clinical staff time spent reviewing data, managing the patient, and communicating with them — and it requires at least one interactive communication (typically a phone or video call) with the patient during the month. 99458 is the add-on for each additional 20 minutes. 99453 is the one-time setup code, and 99454 is the monthly device-supply code. The interactive-communication requirement is the second most common RPM compliance failure after the 99454 16-day threshold and is something the boards reuse.

questions.prompt: An EHR ingests patient-generated blood pressure readings from a home Bluetooth cuff and displays them in the same column as clinic-measured readings, with no visible distinction. A clinician acts on a single elevated home reading by escalating an antihypertensive, and the patient subsequently develops symptomatic hypotension. Which structural failure of the program is MOST responsible?
options: The home device was not FDA-cleared.

The program lacked a provenance and attestation framework — the EHR did not surface the source of each reading or the conditions under which it was taken, so the clinician could not distinguish a calibrated clinic measurement from a single home reading of unknown technique, body position, and time of day.
FHIR does not support blood pressure observations.
The clinician should never act on home blood pressure readings under any circumstances.
questions.rationale: The governing problems of patient-generated health data are provenance (where the data point came from — what device, what conditions, what technique) and attestation (whether the patient took the reading themselves, correctly). FHIR carries device and performer reference fields exactly for this purpose, but the EHR must surface them and the clinician must use them. A program that streams PGHD into the chart with no visible distinction from clinic-measured data is the canonical PGHD failure mode. FDA clearance is not the relevant question (many home cuffs are cleared); FHIR fully supports blood pressure observations; and 'never act on home readings' is wrong — the right answer is to act on them with the right interpretation framework, not to ignore them.

questions.prompt: Which of the following products is MOST LIKELY to be regulated by FDA as a medical device rather than treated as a general wellness product?
options: A smartphone step counter that encourages users to walk 10,000 steps per day
A consumer fitness tracker that estimates calories burned
A continuous glucose monitor (CGM) intended for use by people with diabetes to inform insulin dosing decisions
A meditation app that tracks self-reported mood
questions.rationale: Under FDA's 2016 General Wellness Policy, products intended for general wellness — promoting healthy lifestyle, weight management, fitness, sleep — that present a low risk to user safety are not regulated as medical devices. The first, second, and fourth options fit that description. A continuous glucose monitor intended to inform insulin dosing crosses both lines: its intended use is to support a clinical decision (insulin dosing) and the risk of inaccurate readings is high (insulin dosing errors can be fatal). CGMs are FDA-cleared (Class II for most current models) precisely because of this. The principle the boards reward is that intended use plus risk together determine regulatory status.

questions.prompt: In three or four sentences, define patient-generated health data (PGHD) and explain why provenance and attestation — not data volume — are the governing problems for PGHD integration into the EHR. Give one concrete example of a provenance question a clinician would need answered before acting on a PGHD value.
questions.rationale: A complete answer should define PGHD as health-related data created, recorded, or gathered by or from patients (or family/caregivers) to help address a health concern — including RPM device streams, patient-reported outcomes, smartphone activity data, and patient-entered structured information — distinct from clinically-collected data because the chain of custody runs through the patient rather than a clinician. The governing problem is that the same FHIR Observation field can carry a calibrated clinic measurement and a home reading of unknown technique with no built-in distinction; FHIR has device and performer reference fields exactly for this purpose, but the EHR must surface them. A concrete provenance question: 'Was this blood pressure reading taken on a calibrated arm cuff with the patient seated for five minutes, or on a wrist cuff during a phone call standing up?' Credit any plausible provenance question that turns on device, technique, or conditions of measurement. The point being tested is that PGHD is a data trust problem, not a data volume problem.
